topics.name: Income tax
topics.kicker: Tax on what people earn · Allowed by the 16th Amendment in 1913
topics.briefing: Every spring, millions of Americans fill out forms to figure out how much income tax they owe on the money they earned. The federal government first taxed incomes to help pay for the Civil War, but after the Supreme Court struck down a later income tax in 1895, the country added the 16th Amendment in 1913 to allow it. It became the federal government’s biggest source of money during World War II.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: To pay for Britain’s war against Revolutionary France, Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger introduced this kind of tax in 1799. Britain dropped it after the Napoleonic Wars, but Robert Peel brought it back for good in 1842.
tossups.r: In the United States, the 16th Amendment allowed Congress to collect it. For 10 points, name this tax on people’s earnings.

tossups.p: In _Springer v. United States_, the Supreme Court ruled in 1881 that a wartime version of this tax had been constitutional. An 1862 law that expanded that version also created the office of Commissioner of Internal Revenue.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tax, which Abraham Lincoln first signed into law in 1861 to help pay for the Civil War.

tossups.p: In _Pollock v. Farmers’ Loan & Trust Co._, the Supreme Court struck down this tax in 1895, ruling that it was a direct tax that had to be divided among the states by population. The version it struck down had been part of a tariff law passed the year before.
tossups.r: The 16th Amendment later overcame that ruling. For 10 points, name this tax collected by the IRS.

tossups.p: Grover Cleveland let the Wilson–Gorman Tariff of 1894 become law without his signature, and that law included a 2 percent version of this tax on high earners. Two years earlier, the Populist Party’s Omaha Platform had demanded a graduated version of this tax.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tax that the federal government has collected every year since 1913.

tossups.p: Tennessee congressman Cordell Hull wrote the section of the 1913 Underwood Tariff that brought back this tax, which began at just 1 percent on earnings above $3,000. Woodrow Wilson signed that law months after a new constitutional amendment allowed it.
tossups.r: That amendment was the 16th. For 10 points, name this tax that most Americans file by April 15.

tossups.p: President William Howard Taft supported a constitutional amendment, passed by Congress in 1909, that let the federal government collect this tax without dividing it among the states by population. The amendment was ratified four years later.
tossups.r: That amendment was the 16th. For 10 points, name this tax on wages and other earnings.

tossups.p: Beardsley Ruml, the treasurer of Macy’s department store, pushed for a pay-as-you-go system for this tax, which Congress adopted in the Current Tax Payment Act of 1943. Since then, employers have taken this tax out of each paycheck, a practice called withholding.
tossups.r: Workers get a W-2 form showing how much was withheld. For 10 points, name this tax that Americans report on Form 1040.

tossups.p: In the 1942 Disney cartoon _The New Spirit_, Donald Duck learns that paying this tax on time will help win World War II. That year’s Revenue Act turned this tax into a “mass tax” paid by most working Americans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal tax on people’s earnings, collected by the IRS.

tossups.p: In 1953, the federal bureau that collects this tax got a new name, replacing the word “Bureau” with “Service.” For decades before 1955, the deadline for filing returns for this tax was March 15.
tossups.r: Since then, the usual deadline has been April 15. For 10 points, name this tax collected by the IRS.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Sullivan_, the Supreme Court ruled in 1927 that money earned illegally is still subject to this tax. That decision helped prosecutors convict a Chicago gang boss who had not filed returns for years.
tossups.r: That gangster, Al Capone, was convicted of evading this tax in 1931. For 10 points, name this tax allowed by the 16th Amendment.

tossups.p: The Tax Reform Act of 1986, signed by Ronald Reagan, cut the top rate of this tax to 28 percent and removed millions of poorer families from its rolls. Five years earlier, Reagan’s first big tax law had cut its top rate from 70 to 50 percent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tax that Americans pay on their wages and other earnings, collected by the IRS.

tossups.p: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming are among the states that do not have a state version of this tax on wages, so workers there pay it only to the federal government.
tossups.r: Federal returns for this tax are filed on Form 1040. For 10 points, name this tax on earnings.

tossups.p: The first federal version of this tax in the United States charged 3 percent on yearly earnings over $800, and the next year Congress added a 5 percent rate for higher earners. That wartime version ended in 1872.
tossups.r: It had been passed in 1861 to pay for the Civil War. For 10 points, name this tax revived after the 16th Amendment.

tossups.p: The first Form 1040 was filed in 1914, for money earned in 1913, and fewer than one in a hundred Americans had to fill it out. Like most later versions, it charged higher rates to people who earned more.
tossups.r: That idea is called a progressive tax. For 10 points, name this tax collected by the IRS.

tossups.p: The amendment that lets Congress collect this tax is a single sentence, which says Congress may tax earnings “from whatever source derived.” That amendment was the first of four ratified between 1913 and 1920, during the Progressive Era.
tossups.r: That amendment is the 16th. For 10 points, name this tax that Al Capone was convicted of evading.

trap.title: Tax, tariff, or amendment?
trap.body: Income tax questions are packed with clues that are answer lines of their own. The 16th Amendment is the 1913 change to the Constitution that allowed the tax, and the IRS is the agency that collects it. Before 1913, the federal government got much of its money from tariffs, which are taxes on imported goods. Poll taxes, which kept many Black Southerners from voting until the 24th Amendment banned them in federal elections, are a different tax altogether.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this amendment” wants the 16th Amendment, “this agency” wants the IRS, and “this tax” on wages and earnings wants the income tax. Saying just “taxes” earns a prompt, so add the word “income.”
trap.line: Real answer line: income tax (accept income taxes; prompt on tax or taxes)

topics.name: James Garfield
topics.kicker: 20th U.S. President · Shot just four months into his term (1881)
topics.briefing: James Garfield was born in a log cabin in Ohio, drove canal-boat mules as a teenager, and grew up to be a college leader, a Union general, and a congressman who even invented his own proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Elected president in 1880, he served only about six and a half months. In July 1881, a disappointed office-seeker named Charles Guiteau shot him at a Washington train station, and he died that September from infections his doctors failed to stop.
topics.answerHtml: James Garfield (or James Abram Garfield; do not accept “Chester A. Arthur”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This future president arranged three right triangles to form a trapezoid in a new proof of the Pythagorean theorem, which he published in the _New-England Journal of Education_ in 1876 while serving in Congress.
tossups.r: He was shot just four months into his presidency. For 10 points, name this 20th president, who was assassinated by Charles Guiteau.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man worked on the Ohio and Erie Canal, driving the horses and mules that towed boats along the towpath. He later graduated from Williams College in Massachusetts and became a Union general during the Civil War.
tossups.r: He was the last president born in a log cabin. For 10 points, name this Ohioan who was shot in 1881.

tossups.p: This man taught Latin and Greek at the Western Reserve Eclectic Institute in Ohio and later became its head; the school was renamed Hiram College. He also preached sermons for the Disciples of Christ church.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Ohio Republican who became the 20th president in 1881 and was assassinated months later.

tossups.p: This congressman was one of fifteen members of the Electoral Commission that settled the disputed presidential election of 1876. In January 1880, the Ohio legislature chose him for the U.S. Senate, but he never took that seat.
tossups.r: He succeeded Rutherford B. Hayes as president but was shot by Charles Guiteau in 1881. For 10 points, name this 20th president.

tossups.p: This candidate greeted visitors from the front porch of his farmhouse in Mentor, Ohio, which reporters nicknamed “Lawnfield.” He then narrowly defeated Winfield Scott Hancock, another former Union general, in the 1880 election.
tossups.r: The next year, he was shot by Charles Guiteau. For 10 points, name this 20th president of the United States.

tossups.p: This man went to the 1880 Republican convention to nominate John Sherman, but the delegates deadlocked between Sherman, James G. Blaine, and Ulysses S. Grant. On the 36th ballot, the convention chose this man as a dark-horse nominee instead.
tossups.r: His running mate was Chester Arthur. For 10 points, name this president who was shot in 1881.

tossups.p: This president named William Robertson as Collector of the Port of New York, a choice that led New York senators Roscoe Conkling and Thomas Platt to resign their Senate seats in protest. The New York legislature refused to send either man back to the Senate.
tossups.r: Months later, a supporter of Conkling’s Stalwart faction shot this president. For 10 points, name this man who was killed by Charles Guiteau.

tossups.p: This president backed an investigation of the Star Route frauds, in which officials and contractors cheated the Post Office on mail-delivery routes in the West. His Postmaster General, Thomas James, helped expose the scheme.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who served only about six and a half months before he died in 1881, weeks after he was shot.

tossups.p: Secretary of State James G. Blaine was walking beside this president through the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station when the president was shot. The president had been about to board a train to begin a summer vacation.
tossups.r: The shooter, Charles Guiteau, was a disappointed office-seeker. For 10 points, name this 20th president.

tossups.p: Dr. Willard Bliss, the physician in charge of this president’s care, let doctors search for a bullet without washing their hands or instruments. Alexander Graham Bell built a metal detector to find that bullet, but the device was confused by the metal springs in the president’s bed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who died of infection in September 1881, weeks after Charles Guiteau shot him.

tossups.p: Navy engineers kept this wounded president’s room cool during a hot Washington summer with an early air-conditioning machine that blew air over cloths soaked in ice water. In September, he was moved by train to Elberon, a town on the New Jersey shore, where he died.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who had been shot by Charles Guiteau that July.

tossups.p: This man is the only person ever elected president while serving in the House of Representatives, where he had represented an Ohio district for nearly eighteen years. Before entering Congress, he rose to major general in the Union army and fought at Shiloh and Chickamauga.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Ohio Republican who became the 20th president in 1881 and was shot that July.

tossups.p: When this man took the oath of office in March 1881, his mother, Eliza, became the first mother of a president to attend her son’s inauguration. His father had died when he was a baby, leaving the family poor.
tossups.r: He was born in a log cabin in Ohio. For 10 points, name this president, who served only a few months before he was assassinated.

tossups.p: At his trial, this president’s killer claimed that God had told him to act and that the doctors, not he, had caused the death. The jury rejected his insanity defense, and he was executed in June 1882.
tossups.r: Anger over this president’s death helped pass the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act. For 10 points, name this president killed by Charles Guiteau.

tossups.p: This man’s killer had written a campaign speech supporting him and believed it entitled him to be named U.S. consul in Paris. After the shooting, the killer shouted, “I am a Stalwart of the Stalwarts,” and announced that Chester Arthur would take over as president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, who was shot in a Washington train station in July 1881 and died that September.

Shot by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office-seeker, on July 2, 1881

trap.title: Garfield or his successor?
trap.body: Many Garfield clues also appear in tossups about Chester A. Arthur, his vice president, who took over in September 1881 and signed the Pendleton Act. Garfield is also easy to mix up with William McKinley, another Ohio Republican president who was shot and later died of infection, in Buffalo in 1901. Real answer lines for Arthur say “do not accept James Garfield,” so the reverse mistake costs points too.
trap.fix: Charles Guiteau, the Baltimore and Potomac station, Alexander Graham Bell’s metal detector, and 1881 mean Garfield. Signing the Pendleton Act, the Chinese Exclusion Act, and the “Gentleman Boss” nickname mean Arthur. Leon Czolgosz, Buffalo, and the Pan-American Exposition mean McKinley.
trap.line: Real answer line: James Garfield (or James Abram Garfield; do not accept “Chester A. Arthur”)

topics.name: Jimmy Carter
topics.kicker: 39th U.S. President · Camp David Accords and the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize
topics.briefing: Jimmy Carter grew up on a farm in tiny Plains, Georgia, served on Navy submarines, and ran his family’s peanut business before becoming governor of Georgia and then the 39th president. He helped Egypt and Israel make peace at Camp David, but the Iran hostage crisis and high inflation troubled his presidency, and he lost reelection in 1980. Afterward, he built homes with Habitat for Humanity, won the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize, and died in 2024 at age 100, the longest-lived U.S. president.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young officer in Hyman Rickover’s nuclear submarine program, this man helped clean up after a 1952 accident at a nuclear reactor at Chalk River, Canada. Years later, as president, he toured the Three Mile Island plant after its 1979 accident.
tossups.r: He had left the Navy to run his family’s peanut business in Georgia. For 10 points, name this 39th president.

tossups.p: In a July 1979 television address that critics nicknamed the “malaise speech,” this president warned of a “crisis of confidence” among Americans, though he never actually used the word “malaise.” Days later, he asked his whole cabinet to offer their resignations.
tossups.r: The next year, he lost his reelection race to Ronald Reagan. For 10 points, name this 39th president.

tossups.p: Secretary of State Cyrus Vance resigned in protest over Operation Eagle Claw, an April 1980 mission that ended in disaster when a helicopter crashed into a transport plane in the Iranian desert, killing eight U.S. servicemen.
tossups.r: That mission had tried to rescue Americans held hostage in Tehran. For 10 points, name this president during the Iran hostage crisis.

tossups.p: This president and Leonid Brezhnev signed the SALT II arms treaty in Vienna in 1979, but he pulled it from Senate consideration after the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. He then announced that American athletes would skip the 1980 Moscow Olympics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia Democrat who served as the 39th president of the United States from 1977 to 1981.

tossups.p: On his first full day in office, this president pardoned men who had evaded the draft during the Vietnam War. The day before, he and his family had walked down Pennsylvania Avenue during his inaugural parade instead of riding the whole way in a limousine.
tossups.r: He served one term, from 1977 to 1981. For 10 points, name this president, a former peanut farmer from Plains, Georgia.

tossups.p: This president established full diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China on January 1, 1979, and soon welcomed Deng Xiaoping [“DUNG shyow-PING”] to the White House. That year, he also appointed Paul Volcker to lead the Federal Reserve as prices kept rising.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president whose term was troubled by the Iran hostage crisis.

tossups.p: In his 1980 State of the Union address, this president declared that the United States would use military force if necessary to keep any outside power from controlling the Persian Gulf region. That namesake doctrine answered the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who brought Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin together at Camp David.

tossups.p: Calling the energy crisis “the moral equivalent of war,” this president wore a cardigan sweater in a televised talk urging Americans to turn down their thermostats. He later had solar panels installed on the White House roof.
tossups.r: He also created the Department of Energy in 1977. For 10 points, name this 39th president.

tossups.p: During this president’s term, about 125,000 Cubans sailed to Florida in the Mariel boatlift after Fidel Castro opened a port to anyone who wanted to leave. A year earlier, this president had created FEMA to lead the federal response to disasters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

tossups.p: Senator Ted Kennedy challenged this sitting president for the 1980 Democratic nomination, but this president won enough delegates to be renominated. In the general election, he carried only six states and Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: He lost to Ronald Reagan, whose inauguration came minutes before Iran freed 52 American hostages. For 10 points, name this 39th president.

tossups.p: Shortly before leaving office, this president signed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, which roughly doubled the size of the national park system. He had earlier served one term as governor of Georgia.
tossups.r: He defeated Gerald Ford in 1976. For 10 points, name this Democrat who was president from 1977 to 1981.

tossups.p: Starting in 1984, this former president and his wife, Rosalynn, spent a week almost every year building homes with volunteers for Habitat for Humanity. In 1982, they founded a center in Atlanta that went on to monitor elections and fight diseases such as Guinea worm.
tossups.r: He won the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize. For 10 points, name this former president, who lived to be 100.

tossups.p: For thirteen days in September 1978, this president hosted talks in Maryland’s Catoctin Mountains that led Israel to agree to return the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt. The two other leaders at those talks shared that year’s Nobel Peace Prize.
tossups.r: Those talks produced the Camp David Accords. For 10 points, name this president who helped make peace between Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin.

tossups.p: This president and Omar Torrijos [“tor-EE-hohs”] signed treaties in 1977 that promised to hand the Panama Canal over to Panama by the end of 1999. The Senate approved those treaties in 1978 by just one vote more than the two-thirds needed.
tossups.r: He also created the Department of Education. For 10 points, name this president from Plains, Georgia.

tossups.p: This man titled his 1975 campaign autobiography _Why Not the Best?_, inspired by a question Admiral Hyman Rickover once asked him. He was the first president born in a hospital, and he taught Sunday school for decades at a Baptist church in his hometown.
tossups.r: He died in 2024 at age 100, the longest-lived U.S. president. For 10 points, name this 39th president.

trap.title: Ford, Carter, or Reagan?
trap.body: Carter’s single term sits between Gerald Ford, whom he beat in 1976, and Ronald Reagan, who beat him in 1980. The Iran hostage crisis began under Carter, but the hostages were freed minutes after Reagan took the oath in January 1981, so hostage clues can show up in Reagan questions too. The Camp David Accords and the 1977 canal treaties are also answer lines of their own.
trap.fix: Plains, peanuts, Camp David, the malaise speech, the 1980 Olympic boycott, Habitat for Humanity, and the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize mean Carter. The Iran-Contra affair (secret arms sales to Iran in the 1980s) means Reagan. The pardon of Richard Nixon means Ford.
trap.line: Real answer line: Jimmy Carter (or James Earl Carter Jr.)

topics.name: Panama Canal
topics.kicker: Shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific · Opened by the U.S. in 1914
topics.briefing: Before 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to go all the way around South America. The Panama Canal cut that trip by about 8,000 miles, using giant locks to lift ships about 85 feet up to an artificial lake and back down again. The French tried and failed to dig it, the United States finished it after defeating yellow fever, and Panama took full control of it on December 31, 1999.
topics.answerHtml: Panama Canal (prompt on Panama or canal; do not accept “Suez Canal”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: To steer senators away from a rival route, Philippe Bunau-Varilla [“boo-NOH vah-REE-yah”] mailed each of them a Nicaraguan postage stamp showing an erupting volcano. Bunau-Varilla had worked on an earlier, failed attempt to build this structure, led by the Frenchman Ferdinand de Lesseps.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this waterway that opened in 1914, linking the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

tossups.p: After Colombia’s senate rejected the Hay–Herrán Treaty, a 1903 revolt broke out, and the warship USS _Nashville_ kept Colombian troops from crushing it. The new nation that resulted quickly signed a treaty giving the United States the right to build this structure.
tossups.r: Construction was finished in 1914. For 10 points, name this canal, whose building was championed by Theodore Roosevelt.

tossups.p: The Spooner Act of 1902 authorized buying a French company’s rights to this project for $40 million, but told the president to choose a route through Nicaragua instead if a deal could not be reached.
tossups.r: Theodore Roosevelt later boasted, “I took the Isthmus.” For 10 points, name this canal that opened in 1914.

tossups.p: The Hay–Pauncefote [“PAWNS-foot”] Treaty of 1901 replaced the Clayton–Bulwer Treaty, letting the United States build and control this structure on its own. Three years earlier, the battleship USS _Oregon_ had spent more than two months steaming around South America to reach the Spanish–American War.
tossups.r: Its construction was led by George Goethals. For 10 points, name this canal across Central America, opened in 1914.

tossups.p: Chief engineer John Stevens argued for building this structure with locks instead of at sea level, and he rebuilt a railroad that had crossed the same narrow strip of land since 1855.
tossups.r: Stevens’s successor, George Goethals, finished the job in 1914. For 10 points, name this canal linking two oceans.

tossups.p: Workers building this structure were paid under a “Gold Roll” for most white Americans and a lower-paid “Silver Roll” for most others, including thousands of laborers from Barbados and other Caribbean islands.
tossups.r: Dr. William Gorgas protected those workers from yellow fever by controlling mosquitoes. For 10 points, name this canal that opened in 1914.

tossups.p: In 1928, the adventure writer Richard Halliburton swam the length of this waterway and paid a toll of 36 cents, based on his weight. Ships making the same trip are lifted about 85 feet by locks to cross an artificial lake.
tossups.r: That lake is Gatun Lake. For 10 points, name this waterway that links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

tossups.p: David McCullough told the story of this waterway in _The Path Between the Seas_. Because of the way the land curves, ships moving through it from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travel from northwest to southeast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal, which the United States handed over to its host country at the end of 1999.

tossups.p: Electric locomotives nicknamed “mules” use cables to guide ships through this waterway’s Gatun, Pedro Miguel, and Miraflores Locks. Since 2016, larger ships have used a wider third lane of locks that was added during an expansion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this canal, opened in 1914, whose construction Theodore Roosevelt championed.

tossups.p: In January 1964, a dispute over flying a flag at a high school in the zone surrounding this waterway led to deadly riots, and the host country briefly broke off relations with the United States. Those tensions helped lead to new treaties in 1977.
tossups.r: Those treaties, signed by Jimmy Carter and Omar Torrijos, handed this canal to its host country on December 31, 1999. For 10 points, name this canal.

tossups.p: The steamship SS _Ancon_ made the first official trip through this waterway, and San Francisco held a world’s fair in 1915 partly to celebrate its completion. The waterway’s Atlantic entrance is near the city of Colón.
tossups.r: Its opening on August 15, 1914, drew little notice because World War I had just begun. For 10 points, name this canal.

tossups.p: Building on Walter Reed’s proof that mosquitoes spread yellow fever, Dr. William Gorgas wiped out that disease among the workers building this structure by draining standing water, spreading oil on ponds, and screening buildings.
tossups.r: Army engineer George Goethals led the construction, which was finished in 1914. For 10 points, name this canal linking the Atlantic and Pacific.

tossups.p: Beginning in 1881, a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps [“duh leh-SEPS”] tried to dig this waterway at sea level, but landslides slowed the digging, disease killed thousands of workers, and the company went bankrupt in 1889.
tossups.r: De Lesseps had earlier built the Suez Canal. For 10 points, name this canal that the United States finished in 1914.

tossups.p: The deepest digging for this waterway took place at the Culebra Cut, once named the Gaillard Cut for the engineer who led the work there. Elsewhere, the Gatun Dam blocked the Chagres River, creating what was then the largest artificial lake in the world.
tossups.r: A famous palindrome begins “A man, a plan, a canal” and ends with this canal’s country. For 10 points, name this canal.

tossups.p: A treaty signed by a Frenchman on behalf of a brand-new nation gave the United States control “in perpetuity” of a ten-mile-wide zone for this waterway, in exchange for $10 million and yearly payments.
tossups.r: The United States handed the canal over on December 31, 1999. For 10 points, name this canal, whose construction Theodore Roosevelt championed.

Opened on August 15, 1914, just after World War I began

The U.S. handed it over on December 31, 1999, under treaties Jimmy Carter signed in 1977

A wider third lane of locks opened in 2016 for bigger ships
Philippe Bunau-Varilla mailed senators Nicaraguan stamps showing an erupting volcano to steer them away from Nicaragua
The Spooner Act (1902) authorized buying the French company’s rights for $40 million

trap.title: Suez or Panama?
trap.body: Ferdinand de Lesseps built the Suez Canal in Egypt (opened 1869) and then failed in Panama, so his name shows up in tossups about both canals. The Suez Canal is a sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean and Red Seas, while the Panama Canal uses locks to lift ships across Central America. The Erie Canal (1825), across New York State, is a third canal answer line.
trap.fix: Locks, Gatun Lake, Goethals, Gorgas, Theodore Roosevelt, Colombia, and 1914 mean Panama. Egypt, the Mediterranean and Red Seas, and the 1956 Suez Crisis mean Suez. Saying just “Panama” earns a prompt, so say “Panama Canal.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Panama Canal (prompt on Panama or canal; do not accept “Suez Canal”)

topics.name: John D. Rockefeller
topics.kicker: Founder of Standard Oil · Oil tycoon who gave away hundreds of millions
topics.briefing: John D. Rockefeller started out as a teenage bookkeeper in Cleveland, Ohio, and in 1870 founded the Standard Oil Company, which came to control about 90 percent of America’s oil refining. Critics called him a “robber baron,” and in 1911 the Supreme Court broke his company into 34 pieces. He spent his long retirement giving away hundreds of millions of dollars, funding the University of Chicago and the Rockefeller Foundation, and handing out shiny dimes to people he met.
topics.answerHtml: John D. Rockefeller (or John Davison Rockefeller Sr.; do not accept “Standard Oil” or “John D. Rockefeller Jr.”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1872, this man joined a secret scheme called the South Improvement Company, in which railroads would give big discounts to a few refiners and also pay them part of what rival refiners paid to ship oil. When the plan leaked, oil producers in Pennsylvania organized a boycott, and the state canceled the company’s charter.
tossups.r: His company later controlled about 90 percent of the oil refining in the United States. For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil.

tossups.p: In 1865, this man paid 72,500 dollars at an auction held between him and his partners, the Clark brothers, winning control of a Cleveland oil refinery he ran with chemist Samuel Andrews. Henry Flagler soon joined that business, which was reorganized as a corporation in Ohio in 1870.
tossups.r: That corporation was named Standard Oil. For 10 points, name this man who became the richest American of his time.

tossups.p: For the rest of his life, this man celebrated September 26 as “Job Day,” marking the date in 1855 when he was hired as an assistant bookkeeper by a Cleveland produce firm. He recorded every penny he earned, spent, and gave to his Baptist church in a small notebook he called “Ledger A.”
tossups.r: Fifteen years later, he founded an oil company in that same city. For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil.

tossups.p: This man’s lawyer Samuel C. T. Dodd designed an 1882 agreement in which the owners of dozens of companies handed their stock to nine trustees in return for certificates. That kind of arrangement gave its name to the antitrust laws that were later passed to break up giant businesses.
tossups.r: Ohio’s Supreme Court ordered that trust dissolved in 1892. For 10 points, name this oil tycoon who led the Standard Oil Trust.

tossups.p: Henry H. Rogers, a top executive of this man’s company and a friend of Mark Twain, agreed to meet with a journalist whose father’s oil business in Pennsylvania had suffered from that company’s tactics. Her series in _McClure’s Magazine_ became a famous 1904 work of muckraking.
tossups.r: That journalist, Ida Tarbell, called her book _The History of the Standard Oil Company_. For 10 points, name this man who founded that company.

tossups.p: Henry Demarest Lloyd attacked this man’s business methods in his 1894 book _Wealth Against Commonwealth_. A decade later, Udo Keppler’s cartoon “Next!” showed this man’s company as a giant octopus with its tentacles wrapped around the Capitol and reaching for the White House.
tossups.r: Critics often nicknamed that company “the Octopus.” For 10 points, name this oil tycoon, the founder of Standard Oil.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Edward Douglass White announced the “rule of reason” in a case about this man’s company, which was split up as a result. Two of the pieces later became Exxon and Mobil, which merged again in 1999, and another became Chevron.
tossups.r: That 1911 case broke the company into 34 firms under the Sherman Antitrust Act. For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil.

tossups.p: Baptist minister Frederick T. Gates helped persuade this man to pay for a new university, which opened in 1892 on land donated by the merchant Marshall Field. William Rainey Harper became that school’s first president, and this man went on to give it tens of millions of dollars.
tossups.r: That school is the University of Chicago. For 10 points, name this oil tycoon and philanthropist who founded Standard Oil.

tossups.p: In 1901, this man founded an institute for medical research in New York City that later became a university named for him. In 1909, he paid for a commission that fought hookworm, a parasite that infected many barefoot children across the American South.
tossups.r: In 1913, he created a foundation “to promote the well-being of mankind throughout the world.” For 10 points, name this Standard Oil founder.

tossups.p: A school for Black women in Atlanta took the name Spelman in 1884 to honor the family of this man’s wife, Laura, after he gave it large gifts. In 1902, he created the General Education Board, which spent millions of dollars on schools across the American South.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil, who gave away hundreds of millions of dollars in his long life.

tossups.p: In 1937, this man died at The Casements, his winter home in Ormond Beach, Florida, at the age of 97, about forty years after he had stepped back from running his business. In retirement, he became an avid golfer.
tossups.r: He liked to hand out shiny new dimes to the people he met. For 10 points, name this oil tycoon who founded Standard Oil.

tossups.p: In early 1872, this man’s company bought out 22 of its 26 Cleveland competitors, an episode critics called the “Cleveland Massacre.” He usually offered rival owners either cash or shares of his company’s stock, and those who took the stock often grew rich.
tossups.r: Combining firms that do the same job is called horizontal integration. For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil.

tossups.p: Born in 1839 in Richford, New York, this man moved with his family to the Cleveland area as a teenager. His partner Henry Flagler later built a railroad down Florida’s east coast and turned Palm Beach into a resort.
tossups.r: Flagler and this man had been partners since the 1860s in Cleveland. For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil.

tossups.p: Rival refiners complained that this man’s company slashed prices in their towns until they had to sell out, and that railroads gave it secret discounts called rebates. His company first grew rich selling kerosene, a fuel burned in lamps, before cars made gasoline valuable.
tossups.r: Critics called him a “robber baron.” For 10 points, name this Cleveland businessman who founded Standard Oil in 1870.

tossups.p: Ron Chernow’s 1998 biography _Titan_ tells the story of this man, whose only son built an Art Deco complex of skyscrapers in Midtown Manhattan during the Great Depression. This man’s grandson Nelson later served as vice president under Gerald Ford.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of Standard Oil, often called the richest American in history.

In old age, handed out shiny dimes to children and adults he met
Used horizontal integration: bought up rival refiners that did the same job
Organized the Standard Oil Trust (1882), run by nine trustees; Ohio’s Supreme Court ordered it dissolved in 1892

Got secret railroad discounts called rebates; first grew rich selling kerosene for lamps
By the 1880s his company controlled about 90 percent of U.S. oil refining
Started out in 1855 as an assistant bookkeeper at a Cleveland produce firm
Partner Henry Flagler later built a railroad down Florida’s east coast and developed Palm Beach
Cartoonists drew his company as an octopus, as in Udo Keppler’s 1904 cartoon “Next!”
Companies from the breakup became Exxon, Mobil (the two merged in 1999), and Chevron
South Improvement Company (1872): a secret railroad deal with rebates and payments on rivals’ shipments; Pennsylvania canceled its charter
“Cleveland Massacre” (early 1872): bought out 22 of 26 Cleveland rivals
Won an 1865 auction against partner Maurice Clark ($72,500) for a refinery he ran with chemist Samuel Andrews
Celebrated September 26 as “Job Day”; recorded every penny in “Ledger A”
Lawyer Samuel C. T. Dodd designed the 1882 trust agreement
Executive Henry H. Rogers, a friend of Mark Twain, met with Ida Tarbell
Henry Demarest Lloyd attacked him in _Wealth Against Commonwealth_ (1894)
Chief Justice Edward Douglass White’s “rule of reason” came from the 1911 breakup case
Baptist minister Frederick T. Gates advised his giving; William Rainey Harper was the University of Chicago’s first president
Founded an institute for medical research in New York (1901), now a university; paid for a 1909 hookworm commission
Spelman College in Atlanta honors his wife Laura’s family (1884); created the General Education Board (1902)
Died in 1937, at 97, at The Casements in Ormond Beach, Florida
Born in Richford, New York, in 1839; moved with his family to the Cleveland area as a teenager

trap.title: The man, not the company
trap.body: Standard Oil, the company he founded in 1870, is a separate answer line, and many tossups ask for “this company” or “this trust” instead of the man. The same clues, like Ida Tarbell’s exposé, the South Improvement Company, the octopus cartoon, and the 1911 breakup, show up in both kinds of questions. His son, John D. Rockefeller Jr., and his grandson Nelson Rockefeller, a vice president, are different answers too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man” or “this tycoon” wants Rockefeller, while “this company,” “this trust,” or “this corporation” wants Standard Oil. Among the Gilded Age giants, oil means Rockefeller, steel means Andrew Carnegie, banking means J.P. Morgan, and railroads mean Cornelius Vanderbilt.
trap.line: Real answer lines: John D. Rockefeller (do not accept “John D. Rockefeller Jr.”) and, for the company, Standard Oil Company

topics.name: John Jay
topics.kicker: First Chief Justice of the United States · Diplomat and Federalist author
topics.briefing: John Jay helped negotiate the 1783 Treaty of Paris that ended the American Revolution, wrote five of the _Federalist_ essays, and became the first Chief Justice of the United States in 1789. In 1794 he made a treaty with Britain that was so unpopular that crowds burned him in effigy. As governor of New York, he signed a 1799 law that slowly ended slavery in the state.
topics.answerHtml: John Jay (do not accept “Jay’s Treaty” or “John Marshall”)
reject: treaty of amity commerce and navigation
john jay college of criminal justice

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In _Chisholm v. Georgia_, the Court led by this man ruled that a citizen of one state could sue another state in federal court, a decision that led directly to the Eleventh Amendment. That Court had first met in New York City in February 1790.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man whom George Washington appointed as the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: Late in 1800, John Adams nominated this man to return to a job he had once held, but he turned it down, writing that the Court lacked “energy, weight, and dignity.” Adams then gave that job to his secretary of state, John Marshall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who had been the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: In 1793, the Court led by this man refused to answer a list of questions from Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson about American neutrality in the war between Britain and France, setting the rule that federal courts do not give advisory opinions. This man also had to ride circuit, hearing cases around the country.
tossups.r: He was appointed by George Washington in 1789. For 10 points, name this New Yorker, the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: In 1792, this man won more votes for governor of New York than George Clinton, but officials threw out the ballots from Otsego and two other counties on technicalities, and Clinton kept his office. Three years later, this man was elected governor while he was away in England.
tossups.r: He had gone to London to negotiate a treaty with Britain. For 10 points, name this man, then the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: As governor, this man signed a 1799 law declaring that children born to enslaved mothers after that July 4 would become free at age 28 for males and 25 for females. Years earlier, he had been the first president of the New York Manumission Society, which opened the African Free School.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who also served as the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: In 1786, this man negotiated with Spain’s envoy Diego de Gardoqui [“gar-DOH-kee”] on a trade treaty that would have closed the Mississippi River to American shipping for years, which outraged Southern and Western Americans. He had earlier spent more than two years as an American envoy in Madrid.
tossups.r: He was then the secretary of foreign affairs under the Articles of Confederation. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who became the first Chief Justice.

tossups.p: Distrusting the French foreign minister Vergennes [“ver-ZHEN”], this diplomat persuaded his fellow commissioners to negotiate directly with Britain’s envoy Richard Oswald, even though Congress had told them to consult France first. With Benjamin Franklin and John Adams, he signed the resulting treaty in 1783.
tossups.r: That Treaty of Paris ended the American Revolution. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later became the first Chief Justice.

tossups.p: Illness limited this man to writing just five essays in a famous series: numbers 2 through 5, on the dangers of foreign force and influence, and number 64, on the Senate’s power to approve treaties. Like his two co-authors, he signed those essays “Publius.”
tossups.r: His co-authors were Alexander Hamilton and James Madison. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later became the first Chief Justice.

tossups.p: This man reportedly joked that he could travel the country at night by the light of his own burning effigies after he signed a 1794 agreement with Lord Grenville. That agreement got British soldiers out of their forts in the Northwest Territory but did nothing to stop the British from forcing American sailors into their navy.
tossups.r: Democratic-Republicans hated that treaty, which bears his name. For 10 points, name this diplomat who was then serving as Chief Justice.

tossups.p: This descendant of French Huguenots [“HYOO-guh-nots”] graduated from King’s College, now Columbia University, in 1764 and married Sarah Livingston, a daughter of future New Jersey governor William Livingston. A college of criminal justice in New York City is named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Founding Father who served as the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: This man was the main author of New York’s first state constitution in 1777, and he then became that state’s first chief justice. In late 1778, he was elected president of the Continental Congress, succeeding Henry Laurens of South Carolina.
tossups.r: The next year, Congress sent him to Spain. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later became the first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: The Senate approved a treaty negotiated by this man by a vote of 20 to 10, exactly the two-thirds it needed, after striking out an article that limited American trade with the British West Indies. In 1796, Fisher Ames gave a famous speech urging the House to pay for carrying out that treaty.
tossups.r: That treaty with Britain, signed in 1794, bears this man’s name. For 10 points, name this first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: As a holdover from the Confederation government, this man kept running American foreign policy until Thomas Jefferson arrived in 1790 to lead the new State Department. In 1801, he retired to a farm near Bedford, New York, where he lived until 1829.
tossups.r: George Washington had already named him the first Chief Justice. For 10 points, name this New Yorker.

tossups.p: A 1794 treaty negotiated by this man alarmed Spain, which feared an alliance between Britain and the United States and soon agreed to Pinckney’s Treaty, opening the Mississippi River to American trade. This man negotiated his own treaty in London while he was still serving as a judge.
tossups.r: Thomas Pinckney negotiated the Spanish treaty in 1795. For 10 points, name this first Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: Writing as “A Citizen of New-York,” this man published a 1788 pamphlet urging his state to ratify the Constitution. He then joined Alexander Hamilton at the state’s ratifying convention in Poughkeepsie [“puh-KIP-see”], where the Constitution passed by just three votes.
tossups.r: He had also written five of _The Federalist_ essays. For 10 points, name this man who became the first Chief Justice of the United States.

Spain, fearing an Anglo-American alliance, agreed to Pinckney’s Treaty (1795)

trap.title: The man or his treaty?
trap.body: Some tossups ask for Jay’s Treaty, the 1794 agreement with Britain, instead of the man who negotiated it, and answering “John Jay” to “name this treaty” is wrong. Early buzzers also mix him up with John Marshall, the fourth Chief Justice, who wrote _Marbury v. Madison_, and with his _Federalist_ co-authors Alexander Hamilton and James Madison. Pinckney’s Treaty (1795, with Spain) and the Treaty of Paris (1783) are other treaty traps.
trap.fix: “This man” or “this Chief Justice” wants John Jay; “this treaty” wants Jay’s Treaty. First Chief Justice, the Treaty of Paris, five _Federalist_ essays, and governor of New York mean Jay; _Marbury v. Madison_ and 34 years on the Court mean Marshall.
trap.line: Real answer line: John Jay (do not accept “Jay’s Treaty”)

topics.name: John Tyler
topics.kicker: 10th U.S. President · First VP to become president when a president died
topics.briefing: John Tyler became president in 1841 when William Henry Harrison died after just one month in office, and he insisted he was the real president, not a stand-in, even as critics mocked him as “His Accidency.” His own Whig Party threw him out after he vetoed its bank bills. He signed the resolution to annex Texas, fathered 15 children, and was elected to the Confederate Congress but died in 1862 before he could serve.
topics.answerHtml: John Tyler (do not accept “William Henry Harrison” or “Zachary Taylor”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1833, this man cast the only vote in the Senate against the Force Bill, which let Andrew Jackson use the army against South Carolina during the nullification crisis. Three years later, he resigned from the Senate rather than obey Virginia’s instructions to help erase the Senate’s censure of Jackson.
tossups.r: He later joined the Whigs. For 10 points, name this Virginian who became president in 1841 after William Henry Harrison died.

tossups.p: Fletcher Webster, the son of the Secretary of State, traveled overnight to Williamsburg, Virginia, in April 1841 to bring this man some unexpected news. The next day, Judge William Cranch swore him in at a hotel in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: The news was that William Henry Harrison had died. For 10 points, name this man who became the 10th president.

tossups.p: This man reportedly sent back unopened any letters addressed to the “Acting President,” insisting that he held the office with all of its powers. His view, which became known as the precedent named after him, was finally written into the Constitution by the Twenty-fifth Amendment in 1967.
tossups.r: Critics still mocked him as “His Accidency.” For 10 points, name this first vice president to become president after a president’s death.

tossups.p: In September 1841, every member of this president’s cabinet except Daniel Webster resigned after he vetoed a second bill to create a national bank, a plan pushed by Henry Clay. Days later, a meeting of his own party’s members of Congress expelled him from the party.
tossups.r: That left him a president without a party. For 10 points, name this president who succeeded William Henry Harrison.

tossups.p: In 1843, Virginia congressman John Minor Botts introduced a resolution to impeach this man, the first such attempt against any president, but the House voted it down. Months earlier, a House committee led by John Quincy Adams had condemned this president’s use of the veto.
tossups.r: His opponents were angry about his vetoes of bank bills. For 10 points, name this president who succeeded William Henry Harrison.

tossups.p: On this president’s last full day in office in 1845, Congress overrode his veto of a bill about revenue cutters, small armed ships that enforced customs laws, the first time it had ever overridden a presidential veto. That same day, March 3, Florida became a state.
tossups.r: Two days earlier, he had signed a resolution to annex Texas. For 10 points, name this 10th president.

tossups.p: In 1844, a huge new cannon nicknamed the “Peacemaker” exploded during a demonstration aboard the USS _Princeton_, killing Secretary of State Abel Upshur and Navy Secretary Thomas Gilmer. This president, who was below deck at the time, was unhurt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, who had taken office in 1841 after William Henry Harrison died.

tossups.p: Four months after the USS _Princeton_ disaster killed her father, Julia Gardiner married this man in New York City, making him the first president to marry while in office. His first wife, Letitia, had been the first First Lady to die in the White House.
tossups.r: He had 15 children, more than any other president. For 10 points, name this 10th president.

tossups.p: In 1842, this president applied the Monroe Doctrine to the Hawaiian Islands, warning European powers not to take them over. Two years later, his envoy Caleb Cushing signed the Treaty of Wanghia [“wahng-SHYAH”], the first treaty between the United States and China.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who also signed the joint resolution to annex Texas.

tossups.p: During this president’s term, the Webster–Ashburton Treaty settled the long-disputed border between Maine and the British colony of New Brunswick. The Second Seminole War in Florida also came to an end in 1842, the same year that treaty was signed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, the first vice president to take over after a president died.

tossups.p: After the Senate rejected an annexation treaty negotiated by Secretary of State John C. Calhoun, this president asked Congress to act by joint resolution, which needed only a simple majority in each house. He signed that resolution on March 1, 1845, just days before leaving office.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who began the process of adding Texas to the Union.

tossups.p: This man named his Virginia plantation Sherwood Forest, comparing himself to the outlaw Robin Hood after his party cast him out. In February 1861, he presided over a peace conference in Washington that tried and failed to prevent the Civil War.
tossups.r: Two decades earlier, he had succeeded William Henry Harrison. For 10 points, name this former president.

tossups.p: This man was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives but died in Richmond in January 1862 before he could take his seat. Because he had sided with the Confederacy, the federal government held no official mourning for this former president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 10th president, who had taken office after William Henry Harrison died.

tossups.p: Two grandsons of this president, born in the 1920s, lived into the 21st century, because both he and one of his sons became fathers late in life. This man had 15 children with his two wives, more than any other president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, mocked as “His Accidency” after he succeeded William Henry Harrison.

tossups.p: This man, whose father had also been governor of Virginia, graduated from the College of William & Mary at 17. As president, he served his entire term without a vice president, because the Constitution then had no way to fill an empty vice presidency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who became president when William Henry Harrison died in 1841.

The Webster–Ashburton Treaty (1842) settled the Maine–New Brunswick border

trap.title: Tyler, Harrison, or Taylor?
trap.body: Tyler tossups lean on William Henry Harrison: the 1840 slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too,” Harrison’s one-month presidency, and the Whig ticket they shared. Buzzing “Harrison” on those clues is wrong when the question wants the man who replaced him. Zachary Taylor, the 12th president, has a similar-sounding name and was also a Whig, but he was a general who won the 1848 election and then died in office himself.
trap.fix: Anything after April 4, 1841, like “His Accidency,” the bank vetoes, the cabinet resigning, the USS _Princeton_, and the Texas annexation resolution, means Tyler. Tippecanoe, Tecumseh, and the long inaugural speech mean Harrison; the Mexican War general “Old Rough and Ready” means Taylor.
trap.line: Real answer line: John Tyler (do not accept “William Henry Harrison”)

topics.name: Korean War
topics.kicker: Cold War fight on the Korean Peninsula · Ended by a 1953 armistice
topics.briefing: On June 25, 1950, North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel into South Korea, and the United Nations sent an army, led mostly by Americans, to stop them. After a surprise landing at Inchon, a huge Chinese counterattack, and two more years of grinding battles near the old border, an armistice in July 1953 stopped the fighting. No peace treaty was ever signed, and Americans often call it the “Forgotten War.”
topics.answerHtml: Korean War (accept Korean Conflict or 6–25 War; prompt on Korea or “police action”; do not accept “Vietnam War”)
accept: war to resist america and aid korea
war to resist us aggression and aid korea

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In August 1945, two American officers, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, used a National Geographic map to choose a line dividing a peninsula into American and Soviet occupation zones. Five years later, troops from the northern zone crossed that line, starting this war.
tossups.r: That line was the 38th parallel. For 10 points, name this war that began in June 1950.

tossups.p: The Soviet Union could not veto a key Security Council vote at the start of this war because it was boycotting the council to protest Taiwan’s government holding China’s seat. Sixteen countries eventually sent combat troops to fight under the United Nations flag in this war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which UN forces defended South Korea from 1950 to 1953.

tossups.p: The first American ground troops to fight in this war, a small unit called Task Force Smith, were overrun at Osan in July 1950. By August, the defenders had been pushed into a small corner around the port of Pusan [“POO-sahn”], where they held a line called the Pusan Perimeter.
tossups.r: The invaders had come from North Korea that June. For 10 points, name this war that lasted until 1953.

tossups.p: Some officers warned that one port’s enormous tides and high seawalls made it a terrible place for a landing, but Operation Chromite went ahead there on September 15, 1950. That surprise amphibious attack cut the invaders’ supply lines and led to the recapture of Seoul about two weeks later.
tossups.r: Douglas MacArthur planned that landing at Inchon. For 10 points, name this war, fought from 1950 to 1953.

tossups.p: American F-86 Sabre jets battled Soviet-built MiG-15s over an area near the Yalu River nicknamed “MiG Alley” during this war. In October 1950, Chinese troops under Peng Dehuai [“PUNG duh-HWY”] secretly crossed that river and soon launched huge attacks on UN forces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which China fought on the side of North Korea.

tossups.p: U.S. Marines who fought their way out after Chinese troops surrounded them in bitter, below-zero cold in late 1950 became known as the “Chosin Few.” Afterward, ships carried about 100,000 soldiers and nearly as many civilians away from the port of Hungnam [“HOONG-nahm”].
tossups.r: That fight was the Battle of Chosin Reservoir. For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1953.

tossups.p: In December 1950, Jesse L. Brown, the first African American pilot to complete the U.S. Navy’s flight training program, was shot down near the Chosin Reservoir and died. His wingman, Thomas Hudner, crash-landed his own plane in an attempt to rescue him and received the Medal of Honor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which UN forces fought North Korean and Chinese troops from 1950 to 1953.

tossups.p: House Republican leader Joseph Martin read aloud a letter in which a general in this war wrote that “there is no substitute for victory.” Days later, in April 1951, that general was removed from command for publicly challenging the president’s policy.
tossups.r: That general was Douglas MacArthur, and the president who fired him was Harry Truman. For 10 points, name this war.

tossups.p: Omar Bradley warned that carrying this war into China itself would mean fighting “the wrong war, at the wrong place, at the wrong time, and with the wrong enemy.” Matthew Ridgway, who had taken over the Eighth Army, replaced the fired commander of UN forces in this war.
tossups.r: That fired commander was Douglas MacArthur. For 10 points, name this war that began in June 1950 and ended in 1953.

tossups.p: Truce talks in this war began at Kaesong [“KAY-sung”] in July 1951 and later moved to Panmunjom [“pahn-moon-JUM”], where they dragged on for two years, mostly over whether prisoners of war could refuse to go home. Syngman Rhee [“SING-mun REE”], who wanted to keep fighting, refused to sign the agreement that finally stopped it.
tossups.r: That armistice was signed on July 27, 1953. For 10 points, name this war, which ended without a peace treaty.

tossups.p: During the 1952 presidential campaign, Dwight Eisenhower promised to travel to the front lines of this war, a trip he made that December. After he took office and Joseph Stalin died in March 1953, negotiators finally reached a deal to stop the fighting.
tossups.r: Eisenhower had told voters, “I shall go to Korea.” For 10 points, name this war, ended by an armistice in 1953.

tossups.p: Gregory Peck starred in a 1959 film about the fight for Pork Chop Hill, one of many costly battles over hilltops during this war’s last two years. Other hard-fought battles in this war took place at Heartbreak Ridge and Bloody Ridge, close to the old dividing line.
tossups.r: That line was the 38th parallel. For 10 points, name this war that ended in 1953.

tossups.p: The final episode of a TV comedy set in this war, “Goodbye, Farewell and Amen,” became the most-watched broadcast in American television history up to that time when it aired in 1983. That series followed Hawkeye Pierce and other doctors at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital.
tossups.r: That show, _M*A*S*H_, ran for 11 seasons. For 10 points, name this war in which it was set.

tossups.p: A memorial on the National Mall, dedicated in 1995, shows 19 stainless steel soldiers in rain ponchos walking through a field, and a polished granite wall reflects them to make 38. Nearby, a line carved in stone reads “Freedom Is Not Free.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war, often called the “Forgotten War,” whose memorial stands near the Lincoln Memorial.

tossups.p: A small mare named Reckless carried ammunition for U.S. Marines in this war and was later promoted to staff sergeant. Soon after this war began, Harry Truman approved NSC-68, a secret plan calling for a huge military buildup to contain communism.
tossups.r: During this war, the city of Seoul changed hands four times. For 10 points, name this war fought from 1950 to 1953.

Battles for hills: Pork Chop Hill (a 1959 Gregory Peck film), Heartbreak Ridge, and Bloody Ridge
Its memorial in Washington (1995): 19 steel soldiers in ponchos and the words “Freedom Is Not Free”

trap.title: Korea, not Vietnam
trap.body: The Korean War and the Vietnam War were both Cold War fights between a Communist north and a U.S.-backed south, so players mix them up. Many clues inside Korean War tossups, like Inchon, the Chosin Reservoir, and Douglas MacArthur, are answer lines of their own, and “name this battle” or “name this general” wants that answer instead. Calling it just “Korea” or a “police action” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: The 38th parallel, Inchon, Chosin, MacArthur’s firing, Panmunjom, and _M*A*S*H_ mean Korea (1950–1953). The 17th parallel, Ho Chi Minh, the Gulf of Tonkin, and the Tet Offensive mean Vietnam. Say “Korean War,” not just “Korea.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Korean War (accept Korean Conflict or 6–25 War; prompt on Korea)

topics.name: Labor unions
topics.kicker: Workers banding together for better pay · Knights of Labor, AFL, CIO, UFW
topics.briefing: A labor union is a group of workers who band together to bargain with their employer for better pay, shorter hours, and safer jobs, and who may go on strike when bargaining fails. In the United States, the Knights of Labor, Samuel Gompers’s American Federation of Labor, and John L. Lewis’s CIO led the way, and the Wagner Act of 1935 protected workers’ right to organize. César Chávez and Dolores Huerta later organized farmworkers with the cry “Sí, se puede!”
topics.answerHtml: labor unions (or trade unions or organized labor; do not accept “strikes,” “Pullman Strike,” or “Haymarket affair”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1842 case _Commonwealth v. Hunt_, Massachusetts Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw ruled that these groups were not illegal conspiracies, even when their members refused to work for employers who hired nonmembers. A few years later, Sarah Bagley led a reform association of Lowell mill girls that fought for a ten-hour workday.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organizations of workers, such as the AFL, that bargain with employers for better pay and conditions.

tossups.p: Uriah Stephens founded one of these groups in Philadelphia in 1869 as a secret society, and under Terence Powderly it welcomed women and Black workers and grew to more than 700,000 members. That group, the Knights of Labor, faded after the 1886 Haymarket affair turned many Americans against labor activists.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these workers’ organizations, which use strikes and collective bargaining to win better pay.

tossups.p: A cigar maker born in London led a federation of these groups for nearly forty years, and when asked what workers wanted, he reportedly answered, “More.” His federation, founded in 1886, brought together groups of skilled craft workers and focused on wages and hours.
tossups.r: That leader, Samuel Gompers, headed the American Federation of Labor. For 10 points, name these organizations of workers.

tossups.p: In 1935, mine workers’ leader John L. Lewis, known for his bushy eyebrows, set up a committee to organize every worker in giant industries like steel and autos, skilled or not, and the older federation of craft workers soon expelled his group.
tossups.r: His group, the CIO, merged with the AFL in 1955 under George Meany. For 10 points, name these organizations, which bargain for workers’ pay and benefits.

tossups.p: After the Supreme Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act, Senator Robert Wagner of New York wrote a 1935 law protecting workers’ right to join these groups and bargain collectively. That law created the National Labor Relations Board, which oversees elections in which workers vote on whether one of these groups will represent them.
tossups.r: That law is often called the Wagner Act. For 10 points, name these organizations, such as the United Auto Workers.

tossups.p: A 1947 law passed over Harry Truman’s veto banned the “closed shop,” in which only members of these groups could be hired, and let states pass “right-to-work” laws. That law also let the president seek an 80-day “cooling-off” period to halt a strike that threatened the nation’s health or safety.
tossups.r: That law was the Taft–Hartley Act. For 10 points, name these workers’ organizations, whose activities that law restricted.

tossups.p: Clara Lemlich called for a general strike at a 1909 meeting that launched the “Uprising of the 20,000” among New York shirtwaist makers. Two years later, 146 workers died in the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, a disaster that led New York to pass dozens of new workplace safety laws.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these workers’ organizations, which grew quickly in the garment trade during those years.

tossups.p: In 1892, the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers lost a bitter fight at a Pennsylvania steel mill after Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards and the state sent in its militia. That defeat at Homestead weakened these groups in the steel industry for decades.
tossups.r: The mill belonged to Andrew Carnegie’s company. For 10 points, name these workers’ organizations, which bargain for better pay.

tossups.p: Filipino American grape pickers led by Larry Itliong [“IT-lee-ong”] began a strike near Delano [“duh-LAY-noh”], California, in 1965, and their group soon joined forces with a mostly Mexican American farmworkers’ association. One of that association’s founders later coined the motto “Sí, se puede,” or “Yes, we can.”
tossups.r: That association was founded by César Chávez and Dolores Huerta [“WAIR-tuh”]. For 10 points, name these organizations, such as the United Farm Workers.

tossups.p: In August 1981, Ronald Reagan fired more than 11,000 air traffic controllers who had walked off the job in violation of a federal law, and their group, PATCO, soon lost its legal right to represent them. That defeat is often seen as a turning point that weakened these groups across the country.
tossups.r: Reagan himself had once led one of these groups, the Screen Actors Guild. For 10 points, name these organizations.

tossups.p: In 1903, an Irish-born organizer led a “March of the Mill Children” from Philadelphia to Theodore Roosevelt’s home at Oyster Bay, New York, to protest child labor. A prosecutor once called this organizer for the United Mine Workers “the most dangerous woman in America.”
tossups.r: She was known as Mother Jones. For 10 points, name these workers’ organizations that she spent her life building.

tossups.p: In a 44-day protest that began at the end of 1936, auto workers in Flint, Michigan, refused to leave General Motors plants, a tactic called a sit-down strike. General Motors gave in and recognized the United Auto Workers, one of these groups later led from 1946 to 1970 by Walter Reuther.
tossups.r: Strikes like that one are a main weapon of these groups. For 10 points, name these organizations of workers.

tossups.p: A. Philip Randolph organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925, and in 1937 it became the first of these groups led by African Americans to sign a contract with a major company, the Pullman Company. Randolph later helped plan the 1963 March on Washington.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organizations of workers, which bargain with employers and sometimes go on strike.

tossups.p: The 1932 Norris–La Guardia Act made “yellow-dog contracts,” in which workers promised never to join one of these groups, unenforceable in federal courts. Earlier, Samuel Gompers had called the Clayton Antitrust Act “labor’s Magna Carta” because it said that these groups were not illegal combinations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organizations of workers, which go on strike to win better wages.

tossups.p: When Boston police officers who had formed one of these groups walked off the job in 1919, Governor Calvin Coolidge declared, “There is no right to strike against the public safety by anybody, anywhere, any time.” That same year, a general strike by these groups shut down the city of Seattle for several days.
tossups.r: Steelworkers also struck that year. For 10 points, name these workers’ organizations, which led thousands of strikes in 1919.

Gompers called the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) “labor’s Magna Carta”
