trap.title: Organization or action?
trap.body: Unions are organizations; strikes are one action they take. Some real tossups ask for strikes (“these work stoppages”) instead, and on those, “unions” is wrong, just as “strikes” is wrong here. Famous single events, like the Pullman Strike and the Haymarket affair, and single groups, like the Knights of Labor or the AFL, are separate answer lines too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “these organizations” or “these groups” of workers means unions; “these actions,” “these work stoppages,” or “this tactic” means strikes. If the question names one event or one group (“this strike,” “this federation”), give its name instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: labor unions (or trade unions or organized labor; do not accept “strikes”)

topics.name: Louisiana
topics.kicker: Pelican State on the Gulf Coast · French, Spanish, Cajun, and Creole roots
topics.briefing: Louisiana is the only U.S. state divided into parishes instead of counties, and its laws on property and families still follow the civil-law tradition of France and Spain. Named for the French king Louis XIV, it passed from France to Spain and back again before the United States bought it in 1803. Cajuns, Creoles, Mardi Gras, jazz, and gumbo give it a culture unlike any other state’s, centered on the port city of New Orleans.
topics.answerHtml: Louisiana (accept La Louisiane; do not accept “Louisiana Purchase,” “Louisiana Territory,” or “New Orleans”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In April 1682, René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, reached the mouth of the Mississippi River and claimed its entire basin for France. Later, the brothers Iberville [“EE-ber-vil”] and Bienville [“BYEN-vil”] founded the first French settlements on this colony’s Gulf Coast.
tossups.r: La Salle named the region for King Louis XIV. For 10 points, name this French colony whose name was later given to a U.S. state.

tossups.p: Louis Juchereau de St. Denis founded Natchitoches [“NAK-uh-tish”] in 1714, making it the oldest permanent European settlement in this state. Four years later, Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founded the city that became this state’s largest, naming it for the Duke of Orléans [“or-lay-AHN”].
tossups.r: That city is New Orleans. For 10 points, name this state, whose capital is Baton Rouge.

tossups.p: After France secretly handed this colony to Spain in the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau [“fon-TEN-bloh”], French colonists drove out the Spanish governor Antonio de Ulloa [“oo-YOH-uh”] in 1768. Alejandro O’Reilly crushed that revolt the next year, and a later Spanish governor, Bernardo de Gálvez [“GAHL-vess”], captured British forts during the American Revolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony, which later became the U.S. state whose largest city is New Orleans.

tossups.p: This state was admitted on April 30, 1812, exactly nine years after the signing of the treaty that sold its land to the United States, making it the first state carved out of that land. Before statehood, it had been called the Territory of Orleans.
tossups.r: Its admission came just weeks before the War of 1812 began. For 10 points, name this 18th state, whose capital is Baton Rouge.

tossups.p: Elected bodies called police juries govern many of the 64 parishes in this state, which uses that word instead of “counties.” Its laws on property, contracts, and families are unusual too, following the civil-law tradition of France and Spain instead of English common law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Gulf Coast state, nicknamed the Pelican State, whose capital is Baton Rouge.

tossups.p: Part of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem _Evangeline_ takes place in this state, where thousands of French-speaking Acadians [“uh-KAY-dee-unz”] settled after Britain began forcing them out of Nova Scotia in 1755. Their part of this state is called Acadiana.
tossups.r: Their descendants are called Cajuns. For 10 points, name this state whose largest city is New Orleans.

tossups.p: The Krewe of Comus held the first modern parade of its kind in this state’s largest city in 1857, and in 1872 the Rex organization chose that celebration’s official colors: purple, green, and gold. During the celebration, riders on floats throw beads to crowds, and bakeries sell king cakes.
tossups.r: That celebration is Mardi Gras, or “Fat Tuesday.” For 10 points, name this state, home of New Orleans.

tossups.p: Enslaved and free people of African descent gathered on Sundays to drum and dance at Congo Square, in this state’s largest city. Cornet player Buddy Bolden and pianist Jelly Roll Morton later helped create a new kind of music there.
tossups.r: That music was jazz. For 10 points, name this state whose largest city, New Orleans, was Louis Armstrong’s hometown.

tossups.p: The 34-story capitol of this state, the tallest in the nation, was built at the urging of a governor who was shot inside it in 1935, while serving as a U.S. senator. That man, nicknamed “the Kingfish,” promised “Every Man a King” and proposed a “Share Our Wealth” plan.
tossups.r: That man was Huey Long. For 10 points, name this state, whose capital, Baton Rouge, is home to that building.

tossups.p: Less than a month after a far deadlier storm, Hurricane Rita struck this state’s western coast in September 2005. During that earlier hurricane, thousands of people sheltered in the Superdome, and the government’s slow response was widely criticized.
tossups.r: That earlier storm, Hurricane Katrina, caused levee failures that flooded about 80 percent of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this state.

tossups.p: This state’s flag shows a mother pelican feeding her young above a ribbon with the motto “Union, Justice, Confidence.” That bird had vanished from this state’s coast by the early 1960s, so wildlife officials brought brown pelicans back from Florida.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Gulf Coast state, called the Pelican State and the Bayou State.

tossups.p: The Lake Pontchartrain [“PON-chur-train”] Causeway, which runs about 24 miles across a lake in this state, is often called the world’s longest continuous bridge over water. This state also holds the Atchafalaya [“uh-chaf-uh-LIE-uh”] Basin, the largest river swamp in the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, where the Mississippi River flows past Baton Rouge and New Orleans to the Gulf.

tossups.p: In January 1811, Charles Deslondes [“day-LOHND”] led hundreds of enslaved people in the German Coast Uprising, the largest slave revolt in U.S. history, along the Mississippi River upstream from this future state’s largest city. Militias and U.S. troops put down the revolt within days.
tossups.r: The next year, this territory became a state. For 10 points, name this state, home of New Orleans and the Cajuns.

tossups.p: In 1960, six-year-old Ruby Bridges integrated William Frantz Elementary School in this state, walking past angry crowds with federal marshals, a scene Norman Rockwell later painted. Decades earlier, Homer Plessy had been arrested in this state for sitting in a railroad car reserved for white passengers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, whose segregation law the Supreme Court upheld in _Plessy v. Ferguson_.

tossups.p: Tabasco sauce has been made since 1868 on Avery Island, which sits on top of a huge salt dome in this state. Accordion player Clifton Chenier, called the “King of Zydeco” [“ZY-duh-koh”], made this state’s Creole dance music famous.
tossups.r: Gumbo and jambalaya are also famous dishes from this state. For 10 points, name this state, whose capital is Baton Rouge.

clues.t: Its largest city is New Orleans; its capital is Baton Rouge (“red stick” in French)
Nicknamed the Pelican State (also the Bayou State)
Famous for Mardi Gras, jazz, and foods like gumbo and jambalaya
Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused levee failures that flooded about 80 percent of New Orleans
Its land was part of the 1803 purchase from France, and it was the first state carved from that land
La Salle claimed the Mississippi basin for France in 1682 and named it for King Louis XIV
Brothers Iberville and Bienville founded the first French settlements (1699); Bienville founded New Orleans (1718), naming it for the Duke of Orléans
Became the 18th state on April 30, 1812, after being the Territory of Orleans
Divided into 64 parishes instead of counties
Its laws on property, contracts, and families follow the civil-law tradition of France and Spain, not English common law
Cajuns descend from French-speaking Acadians expelled from Nova Scotia by Britain beginning in 1755
Governor and senator Huey Long (“Every Man a King,” “Share Our Wealth,” “the Kingfish”) was assassinated in 1935
Jazz was born in New Orleans; Louis Armstrong was born there in 1901
Spain ruled it from the 1760s until it secretly returned it to France in 1800 (Treaty of San Ildefonso)
Natchitoches (1714) is its oldest permanent European settlement
France secretly gave it to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)
Colonists drove out Spanish governor Antonio de Ulloa (1768); later governor Bernardo de Gálvez captured British forts in the Revolution
Many of its parishes are governed by elected police juries
Longfellow’s _Evangeline_ is partly set here; the Cajun region is called Acadiana
The Krewe of Comus held the first modern Mardi Gras parade (1857); Rex chose purple, green, and gold (1872)
People of African descent drummed and danced at Congo Square; Buddy Bolden and Jelly Roll Morton were early jazz musicians
Huey Long had its 34-story capitol built, the nation’s tallest; he was shot there in 1935
Its flag shows a pelican feeding her young with the motto “Union, Justice, Confidence”; brown pelicans were brought back from Florida
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway (about 24 miles) is often called the world’s longest continuous bridge over water
The Atchafalaya Basin is the largest river swamp in the United States
German Coast Uprising (1811), led by Charles Deslondes: the largest slave revolt in U.S. history
Ruby Bridges integrated William Frantz Elementary in New Orleans (1960); Homer Plessy was arrested here (1892)
Tabasco sauce comes from Avery Island; Clifton Chenier was the “King of Zydeco”

trap.title: State, purchase, or city?
trap.body: Three answer lines share the same clues. The Louisiana Purchase was the 1803 land deal with France, which covered all or part of 15 states; the state of Louisiana is only its southern corner. New Orleans, its largest city, gets its own tossups about jazz, Mardi Gras, and Hurricane Katrina. Answering “New Orleans” when the question says “this state” is wrong, and plain “Louisiana” only earns a prompt when the question wants the purchase.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this state” or “this colony” wants Louisiana; “this land deal” or “this purchase” wants the Louisiana Purchase; “this city” wants New Orleans. Parishes, Baton Rouge, Huey Long, and the Cajuns usually mean the state.
trap.line: Real answer line: Louisiana (do not accept “Louisiana Purchase” or “New Orleans”)

topics.name: Malcolm X
topics.kicker: Muslim minister and Black nationalist leader · “By any means necessary”
topics.briefing: Malcolm X was born Malcolm Little in Omaha, Nebraska, and educated himself in prison by copying a dictionary by hand, joining the Nation of Islam there. As the group’s outspoken national spokesman, he preached Black pride, self-defense, and separation from white America, and he criticized the nonviolent civil rights movement. After leaving the group and making the hajj to Mecca in 1964, he took the name El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz; he was killed in New York City in February 1965.
topics.answerHtml: Malcolm X (accept Malcolm Little or El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz; prompt on Malcolm alone; do not accept “Elijah Muhammad”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man’s mother was born on the Caribbean island of Grenada, and his father, a Baptist preacher, organized for Marcus Garvey’s movement. Born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1925, this man grew up mostly in and around Lansing, Michigan, where his family was split up in the years after his father’s death.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nation of Islam minister who told his life story to Alex Haley.

tossups.p: While serving a prison sentence for burglary in Massachusetts, this man educated himself by copying an entire dictionary by hand. Letters from his brother Reginald and other relatives drew him to a religious movement, which he joined before his release in 1952.
tossups.r: That movement was the Nation of Islam, led by Elijah Muhammad. For 10 points, name this man who became its most famous minister.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man moved to Boston’s Roxbury neighborhood to live with his half-sister Ella, and later in Harlem he was nicknamed “Detroit Red” for his reddish hair and his Michigan roots. He was sent to prison in 1946 and spent more than six years there.
tossups.r: Like other members of the Nation of Islam, he replaced his last name with a letter standing for his lost African family name. For 10 points, name this man.

tossups.p: Starting in 1954, this man led Temple No. 7 in Harlem, and around 1960 he founded the newspaper _Muhammad Speaks_. Before that, he helped open new temples in Boston and Philadelphia, and as a national spokesman he helped his religious group grow rapidly during the 1950s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nation of Islam minister, who broke with Elijah Muhammad in 1964.

tossups.p: Mike Wallace and Louis Lomax made the 1959 TV documentary _The Hate That Hate Produced_, which introduced millions of viewers to this man and the religious group he spoke for. That group taught that Black Americans should separate from white society and build their own businesses and communities.
tossups.r: That group, led by Elijah Muhammad, was the Nation of Islam. For 10 points, name its most famous spokesman.

tossups.p: After this man said that the assassination of John F. Kennedy was a case of “the chickens coming home to roost,” his religious leader ordered him to stay silent for 90 days. In March 1964, he announced that he was leaving that leader’s movement.
tossups.r: That leader was Elijah Muhammad of the Nation of Islam. For 10 points, name this man, who later founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity.

tossups.p: This man became a friend of a young boxer and visited his training camp in Miami before that boxer won the heavyweight title from Sonny Liston in 1964. The two men split after this man left his religious group, and the boxer, who had taken the name Muhammad Ali, stayed with its leader.
tossups.r: That leader was Elijah Muhammad. For 10 points, name this Muslim minister who told his life story to Alex Haley.

tossups.p: In his 1963 “Message to the Grass Roots” speech in Detroit, this man argued that there is no such thing as a nonviolent revolution. That same year, he mocked the March on Washington as the “Farce on Washington.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nation of Islam minister, a critic of Martin Luther King Jr.’s nonviolent approach.

tossups.p: In an April 1964 speech in Cleveland, this man warned that the year would bring either “the ballot or the bullet,” urging Black Americans to use their votes and to defend themselves. He gave that speech a few weeks after leaving his old religious movement.
tossups.r: That movement was the Nation of Islam. For 10 points, name this Black nationalist leader who was killed in 1965.

tossups.p: In an April 1964 letter, this man described pilgrims “of all colors” worshipping together as equals during a religious journey, an experience he said had changed his thinking about race. He embraced Sunni Islam that year and moved away from the racial teachings of his former group.
tossups.r: That journey was the hajj to Mecca, after which he took a new Muslim name. For 10 points, name this American leader.

tossups.p: At the June 1964 founding rally of a group modeled on the Organization of African Unity, this man promised to win freedom and equality for Black Americans. During a trip through Africa that year, he met Ghana’s president, Kwame Nkrumah.
tossups.r: At that rally, he vowed to win those goals “by any means necessary.” For 10 points, name this founder of the Organization of Afro-American Unity.

tossups.p: This man met Martin Luther King Jr. only once, at the U.S. Capitol in March 1964 during the Senate debate over the Civil Rights Act. In February 1965, he spoke in Selma while King was in jail there, and told Coretta Scott King he hoped to make her husband’s work easier.
tossups.r: Weeks later, he was killed in New York. For 10 points, name this former Nation of Islam spokesman.

tossups.p: In a December 1964 debate at Oxford University in England, this man defended the idea that “extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice,” a line made famous by Barry Goldwater. He also planned to charge the United States with violating human rights before the United Nations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American Muslim leader, who had founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity that June.

tossups.p: In 2021, a New York judge threw out the murder convictions of Muhammad Aziz and Khalil Islam, two men who had each spent about twenty years in prison for this man’s killing, after investigators found that evidence had been withheld. At this man’s funeral, the actor Ossie Davis called him “our own black shining Prince.”
tossups.r: He had been shot as he began a speech at the Audubon Ballroom in February 1965. For 10 points, name this Muslim leader.

tossups.p: Spike Lee directed a 1992 film about this man, with Denzel Washington, who earned an Academy Award nomination, in the title role and Angela Bassett as his wife, Betty. That film was based on a 1965 book published months after this man’s death.
tossups.r: That book was the autobiography he told to Alex Haley, who later wrote _Roots_. For 10 points, name this man.

clues.t: Leading minister and national spokesman of the Nation of Islam under Elijah Muhammad
Told his life story to Alex Haley; the autobiography came out in 1965
Killed on February 21, 1965, at the Audubon Ballroom in New York City
Famous phrase: “by any means necessary”
Made the hajj to Mecca in 1964 and took a new Muslim name
Born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1925; grew up mostly around Lansing, Michigan
In prison (1946–1952), copied a dictionary by hand; his brother Reginald drew him to the Nation of Islam
Replaced his last name with a letter standing for his lost African family name
Left the Nation of Islam in March 1964 and founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity (OAAU)
“The Ballot or the Bullet” speech (April 1964, Cleveland)
Called JFK’s assassination “the chickens coming home to roost”; Elijah Muhammad silenced him for 90 days
Met Martin Luther King Jr. only once, at the U.S. Capitol in March 1964
Friend of the boxer Cassius Clay, who became Muhammad Ali
Spike Lee’s 1992 film about him starred Denzel Washington
His mother was born in Grenada; his father, a Baptist preacher, organized for Marcus Garvey
Lived with half-sister Ella in Boston’s Roxbury; nicknamed “Detroit Red” in Harlem
Led Temple No. 7 in Harlem from 1954; founded the newspaper _Muhammad Speaks_
_The Hate That Hate Produced_ (1959), by Mike Wallace and Louis Lomax, made him nationally known

His letter from Mecca described pilgrims “of all colors” worshipping together as equals

Spoke in Selma (February 1965) while King was jailed; told Coretta Scott King he hoped to make King’s work easier
Debated at Oxford (December 1964), defending “extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice”
Planned to charge the United States with human rights violations at the United Nations
In 2021, a judge threw out the convictions of Muhammad Aziz and Khalil Islam for his killing
Actor Ossie Davis’s eulogy called him “our own black shining Prince”
Married Betty Sanders in 1958; they had six daughters

trap.title: Minister, mentor, or rival?
trap.body: Malcolm X tossups are full of other famous names that are answer lines too: Elijah Muhammad, who led the Nation of Islam; Martin Luther King Jr., whose nonviolence he criticized; Muhammad Ali, the boxer he befriended; and Alex Haley, who wrote down his life story. Buzzing with a name you just heard in the clue loses the points. His other names, Malcolm Little and El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, are accepted.
trap.fix: Ask who the clue is really about. “This man” who copied a dictionary in prison, led Temple No. 7, made the hajj in 1964, and was killed at the Audubon Ballroom is Malcolm X. The leader of the whole Nation of Islam from the 1930s to 1975, based in Chicago, is Elijah Muhammad.
trap.line: Real answer line: Malcolm X (accept Malcolm Little or El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz)

topics.name: Martin Van Buren
topics.kicker: 8th U.S. President · Andrew Jackson’s vice president and the “Little Magician”
topics.briefing: Martin Van Buren, born in 1782 in the Dutch-speaking village of Kinderhook, New York, was the first president born a citizen of the United States instead of a British subject. A master politician nicknamed the “Little Magician,” he helped build the Democratic Party and served as Andrew Jackson’s vice president before winning the presidency in 1836. The Panic of 1837 hit just weeks after he took office, and voters turned him out four years later.
topics.answerHtml: Martin Van Buren (do not accept “Andrew Jackson” or “William Henry Harrison”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1832, Vice President John C. Calhoun broke a tie to block this man’s appointment as minister to Great Britain, a snub that backfired and won this man sympathy. A year earlier, this man had resigned as Secretary of State during the Petticoat Affair.
tossups.r: Later that year he was elected Andrew Jackson’s vice president. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who became the eighth president.

tossups.p: William Marcy, a member of this man’s political machine called the Albany Regency, defended the spoils system by declaring that “to the victor belong the spoils.” This man’s faction, the Bucktails, had earlier fought New York governor DeWitt Clinton for control of the state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York politician nicknamed the “Little Magician,” who became the eighth president.

tossups.p: In an 1827 letter to Virginia newspaper editor Thomas Ritchie, this man proposed rebuilding an alliance between “the planters of the South and the plain Republicans of the North.” That plan helped create the party that elected Andrew Jackson president the next year.
tossups.r: That party became the Democrats. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who succeeded Jackson as president in 1837.

tossups.p: In one election, this man defeated several regional candidates from a new opposition party, including William Henry Harrison, Hugh Lawson White, and Daniel Webster. His running mate, Richard Mentor Johnson, fell short of an electoral majority and became the only vice president ever chosen by the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who won the election of 1836, becoming the eighth president of the United States.

tossups.p: Just weeks after this man took office, banks in New York stopped paying out gold and silver, setting off a depression that lasted for years. Many people blamed his predecessor’s Specie Circular, which had required buyers of public land to pay in gold or silver.
tossups.r: That crisis was the Panic of 1837. For 10 points, name this eighth president, Andrew Jackson’s successor.

tossups.p: This president’s answer to a financial crisis was to keep federal money in government vaults instead of private banks, a “divorce” of the government from the banks. He signed the act creating that system on July 4, 1840, but the Whigs repealed it the next year.
tossups.r: That system was called the Independent Treasury. For 10 points, name this president who faced the Panic of 1837.

tossups.p: After British and Canadian forces set fire to the American steamboat _Caroline_ on the Niagara River in 1837, this president sent General Winfield Scott to calm the border. Scott also helped end the bloodless Aroostook [“uh-ROO-stuk”] War, a dispute over timberland between Maine and New Brunswick, during this man’s term.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this one-term president, who served between Andrew Jackson and William Henry Harrison in the late 1830s.

tossups.p: This president’s administration argued that Africans who had taken over the Spanish ship _La Amistad_ should be handed over to Spanish authorities in Cuba. In 1841, days after he left office, John Quincy Adams won their freedom before the Supreme Court.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president, who had lost his bid for reelection to William Henry Harrison.

tossups.p: Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote an open letter in 1838 pleading with this president not to enforce a removal treaty, but that year soldiers under General Winfield Scott forced thousands of Cherokee people out of their homes and onto the road west. Most of them did not reach Indian Territory until early 1839.
tossups.r: That forced march became known as the Trail of Tears. For 10 points, name this president, who had been Andrew Jackson’s vice president.

tossups.p: Pennsylvania congressman Charles Ogle attacked this president in the 1840 “Gold Spoon Oration,” claiming that he lived like a king in a lavishly decorated White House. That year, his opponents portrayed their own candidate as a plain man of log cabins and hard cider.
tossups.r: Whigs chanted “Van, Van, is a used-up man.” For 10 points, name this president who lost to William Henry Harrison in 1840.

tossups.p: Supporters of this man formed “O.K. Clubs” in 1840, named for his nickname “Old Kinderhook,” which helped spread a popular two-letter expression. He grew up speaking Dutch in his New York hometown, where his father ran a tavern.
tossups.r: He was the first president born a citizen of the United States. For 10 points, name this eighth president.

tossups.p: In 1844, this former president lost the support of many Southern Democrats when he published a letter opposing the immediate annexation of Texas. Unable to win two-thirds of the delegates at his party’s convention, he lost the nomination to the dark horse James K. Polk.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker, who had served one term as president from 1837 to 1841.

tossups.p: In 1848, this former president ran again with Charles Francis Adams as his running mate, winning about ten percent of the popular vote but no electoral votes. Antislavery New York Democrats nicknamed “Barnburners” backed that campaign, which split the Democratic vote and may have helped Zachary Taylor win.
tossups.r: He ran as the candidate of the Free Soil Party. For 10 points, name this man who had been the eighth president.

tossups.p: In 1840, this president ordered a ten-hour workday for laborers on federal public works projects. Earlier in his term, he turned down the Republic of Texas’s request to join the United States, fearing a war with Mexico and a fight over slavery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this eighth president, whose term began with the Panic of 1837.

tossups.p: Because this president’s wife, Hannah, had died in 1819, his daughter-in-law Angelica Singleton, a relative of Dolley Madison, served as White House hostess. In retirement, he lived at Lindenwald, his estate in Kinderhook, New York, where he died in 1862.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this eighth president, known for his bushy sideburns and the nickname “the Little Magician.”

Andrew Jackson’s second vice president (1833–1837) and chosen successor

The first president born a citizen of the United States (1782) instead of a British subject

Grew up speaking Dutch in Kinderhook, New York, where his father ran a tavern

His nickname “Old Kinderhook” helped spread the expression “OK” (O.K. Clubs, 1840)

His administration wanted the _Amistad_ Africans handed over to Spanish authorities
Ralph Waldo Emerson’s 1838 open letter begged him not to remove the Cherokee
Charles Ogle’s “Gold Spoon Oration” (1840) attacked his White House lifestyle; Whigs chanted “Van, Van, is a used-up man”

Ordered a ten-hour day for laborers on federal public works (1840); refused Texas’s request to join (1837)

trap.title: Jackson’s heir, not Jackson
trap.body: Van Buren spent his career at Andrew Jackson’s side as secretary of state, vice president, and chosen successor, so his tossups are full of Jackson clues like the Petticoat Affair, the Bank War, and Indian removal. The Trail of Tears is a common trap: Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, but most Cherokees were forced west in 1838–1839, while Van Buren was president. William Henry Harrison, who beat him in 1840, is another wrong buzz.
trap.fix: The Panic of 1837, the Independent Treasury, the _Caroline_ and _Amistad_ affairs, Kinderhook, and the 1848 Free Soil run mean Van Buren. Vetoing the national bank’s recharter, the Battle of New Orleans, and signing the Indian Removal Act mean Jackson.
trap.line: Real answer line: Martin Van Buren (do not accept “Andrew Jackson”)
